1   Introduction
Sparsification refers to the general procedure by which a large, complex object is replaced by
an ideally much smaller object which nevertheless preserves certain properties of interest. Such
sparsification was first introduced (independently) in the work of Benczúr and Karger [BK96] and
Talagrand [Tal90]. [BK96] studied the so-called cut sparsification of graphs G = (V, E, w) where the
goal is to select a subset of the edges of the graph, while still preserving all of the cut-sizes. [Tal90]
instead studied a continuous generalization of this notion called ℓ1 -norm sparsification, where
one is provided with a sum of ℓ1 norms of linear functions, and wishes to choose a subset which
preserves the sum on every input.
    Since these seminal works, sparsification has evolved into a rich field. The works of Spielman
and Teng [ST11], Spielman and Srivastava [SS11], and Batson, Spielman, and Srivastava [BSS14]
generalized cut sparsification of graphs to a stronger notion called spectral sparsification. These
notions of graph sparsification have proved to be useful in a plethora of algorithmic applications,
ranging from graphs [BK96, ST04, SS11], to linear system solving [ST04], and numerous problems
in the graph streaming literature [AGM12a, AGM12b, McG14, ADK+ 16, KLM+ 17, KMM+ 19].
    Other works have sought to understand the theoretical limits of which objects can be sparsified.
This exploration began with the study of hypergraph cut sparsification and CSP sparsification
in the work of [KK15], which led to works improving sparsifier sizes [CKN20], a study of spec-
tral hypergraph sparsification [SY19, KKTY21a, KKTY21b, Lee23, JLS23], sparsification of codes
[KPS24a, KPS25, BG25, BGP26, KPS26, LMW26], as well as other generalizations like sparsifying
sums of norms [JLLS23], and sparsifying sums of PSD matrices [HLM+ 26, BKLM26, BKMT26].
    Despite this vast attention devoted to sparsification, there is one common thread which
plagues almost all of these works: random sampling. Indeed, in all instances of sparsification
via random sampling, there is an inherent blow-up (in the size of the sparsifier) which scales as
log(dim). For instance, in the cut-sparsification of graphs of [BK96], this led to sparsifiers preserving
Oε (|V | log(|V |)) many edges, and in the work of [Tal90], this led to ℓ1 -norm sparsifiers preserving
Oε (n log n) many terms. Removing these extra logarithmic factors remained an open question for
the ensuing years. Only in the work of Batson, Spielman, and Srivastava [BSS14] was this first
resolved for cut (and in fact, the stronger notion of spectral) sparsification, whereby they produced
sparsifiers which retained only Oε (n) many edges. For ℓ1 norms, this remained open much longer,
until the very recent work of Reis and Rothvoss [RR26], which produced ℓ1 -norm sparsifiers with
only Oε (n) many terms. Along the way, the only other distinct instances of sparsification that avoid
this inherent logarithmic factor are due to De Carli Silva, Harvey and Sato [SHS15] on sparsifying
sums of PSD matrices (and hypergraph cut sparsification for arity r = 3), and the (even more)
recent work of Basu, Kothari, Meka and Tudose [BKMT26] which extends [RR26] to sparsifying
Abelian Cayley graphs.
    In this work, we re-visit the framework of Reis and Rothvoss [RR26] and ask just how far it can
be pushed in constructing optimal size sparsifiers.

1.1   Our Results
As our main result, we show that the framework of [RR26] can be extended to imply optimal
sparsification for sums of support functions of centrally symmetric, compact, convex sets a.k.a., symmetric
convex bodies1 . More formally, one can consider the space E = Rn . A set Ci ⊆ E is said to be:

   1. Centrally symmetric if whenever x ∈ Ci , then −x ∈ Ci .

proper convex bodies in Rn .

In this section, we now adapt the results from the previous section to building seminorm sparsifiers.
We first recall the definition of a seminorm:

Definition 5.1. A function f : Rn → R⩾0 is said to be a seminorm if it satisfies the following

(1) Positive Homogeneity. For all x ∈ Rn and λ ∈ R, f (λx) = |λ| · f (x).
